# Khantīvādījātaka (Ja 313)

**ID:** Ja 313
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Khantīvādījātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Khantīvādījātaka* (Ja 313) is a canonical birth-story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon, titled *The Teacher of Patience* in modern translation. According to its framing narrative, the Buddha recounted the tale while residing at Jetavana concerning an easily angered monk. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born into a wealthy brahman family as Kundaka, but renounces worldly life to become an ascetic sage (*isi*) known as the "Preacher of Patience" (*Khantivādin*) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Nattier 2009; Readings from the Jatakas]. While King Kalābu of Benares sleeps during a drunken revel in his royal pleasure garden, his female attendants wander off to listen to the Bodhisatta's teaching [Readings from the Jatakas]. Awaking in a rage, the king confronts the sage and interrogates him regarding patience—defined by the Bodhisatta as maintaining freedom from anger when reviled, struck, or insulted [Harvey 2000; Readings from the Jatakas]. Resolving to test this virtue, the king commands his executioner to flog the Bodhisatta with thorny whips and sever his hands, feet, nose, and ears [Winternitz 1933; Appleton 2010; War Yar Mein Da 2015; Readings from the Jatakas]. The Bodhisatta endures the mutilation without malice, declaring that his patience resides deep within his heart rather than in his skin, while the king is swallowed by the earth and reborn in hell [Hazra 1994; Readings from the Jatakas].

The story is widely cited in Buddhist literature as a quintessential illustration of the perfection of patience or forbearance (*khanti* / *kṣānti*) through extreme physical endurance and the radical "giving up of the body" (*ātmabhāva-parityāga*) [Harvey 2000; Appleton 2010; Nattier 2009]. In ancient Indian art, scenes from the narrative are attested as early as the third century BCE on a relief at the Sañcī Stupa, as well as across Gandharan sculptural reliefs [Winternitz 1933]. Modern scholarship has analyzed the story in terms of the conflict between external worldly dominance and internal spiritual mastery [MacQueen, cited in Martin 2006; Fenn 1994].
